events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, would you look at this place! I declare, it's like stepping into one of Grandmother's old daguerreotypes — all dust and grandeur and secrets just waiting to be shaken loose. Vincent, darling, tell me you've already found something peculiar, because my fingers are positively itching. And James Hartwell, I see that look on your face — you're already three steps ahead of the rest of us, aren't you? Boys, don't you dare touch that chandelier, it looks like it's hanging on by sheer stubbornness and a prayer.
events.thinking: The foyer opens around me and my chest does that thing — that cave-mouth lift, breath widening before I've decided to breathe. Dust motes in the chandelier light. The portraits are watching. My fingers are already warm, already wanting to touch the bannister, the guest book, the edges of things. But first — oh, there they are. Vincent, solid as a stone wall, and my stomach settles just seeing him the way it always does, the way it did when I was eleven and he waited at the school gate. James — something behind my ribs brightens, a quick heat I don't examine yet. And the Boys, my boys, grinning like they've already cased the place. The ache and the lightness meet somewhere under my sternum. Everyone's here. Everyone's whole. The prickling starts at my scalp — the diamond, the puzzles, the locked-box feeling — but it can wait one more breath. Let me just stand in this doorway and feel them all in the room with me before the adventure swallows us.

events.desc: The guest book is sitting right there, open and waiting. Every good mystery starts with knowing who else has walked through the door before you. And that chandelier — Lord have mercy, one good sneeze and we're all wearing crystal.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor! I am Pemberton, the estate manager. I do hope your journey was not too arduous. If I may direct your attention to the guest book — it is tradition, you see, for all visitors to sign upon arrival. The late master was most particular about such things. Please, do make yourselves comfortable — I shall ensure everything is in perfect order for the treasure hunt. Every room has been prepared, every corridor dusted. Well... mostly dusted. The manor is rather extensive, I'm afraid.
events.thinking:
The cold weight settles behind my sternum as I survey the entrance hall. Clara is right here — trusting, oblivious, skipping through rooms that should have been mine. My fingers feel precise, architectural. Every person in this room is a piece on a board I've already mapped.

But I must be careful. The Brixton Boys watch too closely — I feel that prickle along my neck when their eyes track me. And James Hartwell, that earnest fool, hovering near Clara like a loyal hound. Predictable, but an obstacle.

First things first. I am Pemberton. The mild-mannered estate manager. Obsequious. Helpful. The man who opens doors and fetches tea. That is the mask, and the mask must be flawless before I can begin to work beneath it.

The guest book — that's my opening. A perfectly natural thing for an estate manager to attend to. It lets me position myself, take stock of the room, and begin to map the soft points. Who defers to whom. Who watches. Who trusts.

My jaw is tight but my smile is ready. The housekeeper's smile — the one that makes compliance feel like their idea. I can feel it forming already, warm and professionally solicitous, before I've decided to wear it.

The treasure hunt is secondary. Clara is primary. But the hunt gives me proximity, gives me reason to guide her into isolated rooms, toward precarious chandeliers and unstable architecture. The manor itself can be my instrument — nothing so crude as direct action. The scheme must be elaborate. Theatrical. Beautiful.

For now: establish Pemberton. Greet the guests. Learn the terrain.

events.desc: Look at them. Every one of them a piece on my board. Clara smiles at me with that trusting, open face — the same face her mother wore, the same face that inherits everything while I receive nothing but the privilege of service. Enjoy the entrance hall, dear cousin. By the time this hunt is over, the only treasure anyone will find is the beautiful inevitability of my design.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Right. We're here. Doily Manor. The lads are back at the van, told 'em to wait till I scouted the place. And there she is — Clara. My Clara. Well, not MY Clara, but... you know what I mean. The old man's girl. Promised him on his deathbed, didn't I? 'Look after her, Danny.' And I said I would. And here I am.

Now then. Who else is in here? Vincent Marsh — that's Pemberton's mate, isn't it? Something about him makes the back of my neck go all prickly. Too smooth. Too... polished. Like a new penny in a gutter. Nobody's that clean without hiding something dirty underneath. And he's standing near Clara. TOO near Clara. My shoulders are already squaring up.

James Hartwell — him I don't mind so much. Solid bloke. Means well. Got that look about him like he'd step in if things went sideways. Could be useful.

The entrance hall... big, dusty, chandelier hanging like it's had enough of life. Portraits of dead people staring down at us. The coat rack by the door looks like it'd fall over if you breathed on it.

My gut's doing that thing. That tightening. The same one from when I was ten and that bloke in the clean suit came round. Something ain't right about this place. Can't put my finger on it yet. But my body knows. It always knows before my brain catches up.

I should have a look around. Get the lay of the land. But I don't want to leave Clara alone with Marsh. Not yet. Let me say hello first, let her know I'm here. Let Marsh know I'm watching.

events.desc: Look at Marsh over there, all neat and tidy like a cat that's already eaten the canary. I can't say nothing yet — I ain't got nothing solid. But my neck's prickling something fierce, and that prickle ain't never been wrong. Not since I was fifteen and that new kid was laughing too easy. Three weeks later, gone with the stash. I see you, Marsh. I see you standing too close.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah, Doily Manor at last! You know, I was personally invited by the late Lord Doily himself — well, his solicitor, which amounts to the same thing. Gave me the grand tour years ago, in fact. Marvellous place. The treasure? Oh yes, I know *all* about it. The old boy practically told me where it was over brandy one evening. But first things first — let's see who's signed in, shall we?
events.thinking: Just arrived at Doily Manor. My chest is already doing that thing — the hollow pull behind my navel, fingers curling slightly, eyes scanning. Four people in the entrance hall. Clara Bellingham, Vincent Marsh, the Brixton Boys, James Hartwell. That's a lot of witnesses, which is a lot of potential dupes. The guest book is interactable — could have clues about the manor, previous visitors, maybe hints about where the treasure is. The library and kitchen are accessible. Library screams 'hidden clues' — carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription, bookshelves. That's where secrets live. But first — information. The guest book might tell me something useful, or at least give me a story to spin. I've got this fake medal in my pocket. Beautiful. The cool tightness behind my eyes is already working — who here is gullible, who's a threat, who can I send on a wild goose chase while I slip away? My body is already composing the architecture. The entrance hall is the staging ground. I need to look casual, establish authority, and gather intelligence before anyone else gets organized. The guest book first — INTERACT with it, see what it reveals. Meanwhile, I can posture for the crowd.

events.desc: Not a word of that is true, naturally. Never met Lord Doily. Never been within fifty miles of this heap. But confidence is nine-tenths of the law, and the other tenth is knowing when to run. Now — that guest book might actually be useful, and while these fools are still gawping at the chandelier, Reginald Foxworth will be three steps ahead. As always.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, portraits staring down like disapproving uncles. And there she is — Clara. My chest does that thing again, that shift, like gravity briefly forgot which direction was down and then remembered, harder. She's standing near the others and I'm acutely aware of the distance between us — seven feet, maybe eight. My shoulders have already drawn back. I'm standing taller than I need to.

Vincent Marsh is here too. The back of my neck prickles. I can't prove anything about the man, but something about the way he positions himself — always slightly too close to Clara, always slightly too aware of the room's exits. I should give him the benefit of the doubt. Father would. Father always did. The stranger on the road, the handshake, driving off. Trust first.

But my body doesn't trust him. My body is tracking him the way it tracks a loose hinge.

The Brixton Boys — boisterous, unpredictable. Reginald Foxworth — I know the type. Old money, easy charm. The kind of man who makes a room laugh without building anything.

A guest book on the side table. That's... that's an opportunity. Sign it with flourish. Show Clara I'm the sort of man who observes the proprieties. No — better. Examine it first. There might be something useful in there — previous guests, clues about this manor. That serves both goals: gallantry through thoroughness, and a step toward the treasure.

My hands want to be busy. They always want to be busy. Three nights building that bridge — my hands remember that. They want to build something here too. But first, establish presence. Let Clara see that James Hartwell arrived and immediately began investigating.

events.desc: James Hartwell surveys the foyer with the practiced eye of a man who has read fourteen books on Victorian architecture in the past week. He notes the chandelier, the dust patterns, the load-bearing capacity of the staircase — all while positioning himself, quite unconsciously, between Clara and the nearest shadow.

Clara Bellingham: James, darling, you are an absolute treasure yourself — floor plans AND county records? I should have known you'd arrive with a research library in your back pocket. Now, let's see what this guest book has to tell us. Every person who's walked through that door left a little piece of themselves on these pages, and I intend to read every last word. Reginald, honey, if Lord Doily really did tell you where the diamond is over brandy, you are welcome to lead the way — but I have a feeling this old house has a few surprises even you haven't accounted for. And Boys — thank you. For coming. For always coming.
events.thinking: The guest book — my fingers found it before my mind caught up, the leather warm and cracked under my thumb the way Grandmother's old letters felt. James already had his hands on it too, bless him and his county records. Everyone's settling into the foyer like puzzle pieces finding their edges. Vincent introduced himself as Pemberton — wait. No. Vincent IS Vincent. Pemberton is the estate manager. But Vincent just said... my stomach does a small confused flip but it smooths out almost immediately. Of course he's playing along, or I misheard, or — no, it doesn't matter. Reginald is already puffing up like a rooster about being personally invited, claiming he knows where the treasure is. My scalp prickles — does he really? The locked-box feeling intensifies. The Boys are here, solid and warm, and James is being wonderfully James about the whole thing, all checklists and chandelier angles. The library catches my eye from here — floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, a carved mantelpiece with an inscription. An inscription. My hands are already warm. That's where the first clue will be, I can feel it the way I felt the crystal formation before I saw it. But I should look at this guest book properly first — who else has been here? What names are written? The prickling won't let me skip a step.

events.desc: Reginald claims to know all about the treasure. Bless his heart, he probably believes it too. But the library — that inscription on the mantelpiece is calling to me like Grandmother's locked box. First the guest book, then the library. One key at a time, Clara.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Ah, splendid — I see Mr Hartwell has already taken the initiative with the guest book. Most thorough, sir, most thorough indeed. Now then, if I might suggest — the library would be the natural place to begin the hunt proper. The late master spent most of his time there, and the mantelpiece bears an inscription that has puzzled visitors for decades. I have taken the liberty of leaving the doors unlocked, of course. Shall I lead the way? The corridors can be rather... disorienting for newcomers.
events.thinking:
Clara called me 'Vincent, darling' — she used my real name. A flicker of heat at the back of my neck. But no — she knows me as Pemberton. She must have said it casually, the way she says everything, throwing names around like confetti. Wait. She said 'Vincent.' Does she know? No. No, she's too trusting for that. She probably heard the name somewhere in the estate papers. I need to deflect. Pemberton would not react to being called Vincent — he wouldn't even notice, because it isn't his name.

My shoulders tightened when she said it. I felt the prickle — the boy-with-the-sandwich feeling, the sense of being seen before I'd composed myself. But it passed. She's already moved on to chattering about chandeliers and daguerreotypes. She doesn't know. She can't know.

Now — James Hartwell has gone straight to the guest book. Predictable. Methodical. He'll find nothing there but names and dates. Reginald is blustering about being personally invited by Lord Doily — useful fool, that one. The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara. That's the prickle again. What did they say? What are they watching?

The library. That's where I need to be. The carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that's where the first real clue will be. If I can get there before the others, I can read it, understand it, and then decide what version of it to share. The estate manager would naturally suggest the library as the first stop on the treasure hunt. It's the most logical room. Pemberton is nothing if not logical.

But I need to separate Clara from her protectors. Not yet — too soon. First, establish the rhythm. Be helpful. Be indispensable. Guide the hunt. And guide Clara toward the parts of the manor where chandeliers hang precariously and staircases creak in just the wrong places.

The library first. Always the library first.

events.desc: She called me Vincent. My skin is still prickling. But she smiled when she said it — that open, careless smile that sees nothing beneath surfaces. She doesn't know. She simply stumbled across a name in a ledger somewhere and attached it to a face. The way she attaches everything — carelessly, warmly, without checking whether the thing she's holding has teeth. I shall lead them to the library, and I shall read that inscription before any of them can puzzle out its meaning. Knowledge is the only currency that matters in a treasure hunt — and I intend to be the central bank.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Oi, Clara love, do us a favour and step away from under that chandelier, would you? The thing's hanging on by a thread and a prayer, and I ain't about to explain to your old dad — God rest him — that I let a light fixture do what the streets of Brixton never managed. Hartwell's got the right idea with that guest book — let's see who's been poking around this place before us. And Mister Pemberton, sir — no offence meant — but when you say every room's been 'prepared,' what exactly does that mean? I mean, is it 'prepared' like tidied up, or 'prepared' like... set up? Because there's a difference, innit. Not that I'm saying anything's wrong! Just... asking. Danny asks questions. That's what Danny does.
events.thinking:
Right, so I've had a look round. Clara's talking — bless her, she's already excited, fingers itching for treasure and adventure. That's Clara all over. Her old man was the same, couldn't sit still, always poking into things that didn't want to be poked.

Now then. Pemberton — or Marsh, whatever his name is — he's done his little welcome speech. 'Every room has been prepared, every corridor dusted.' Has it now? Prepared for what, exactly? And why's he so keen for everyone to sign the guest book? Tradition, he says. The late master was 'most particular.' My neck's prickling again. Not hard, not like alarm bells, but that steady hum that says 'watch this one.'

But here's the thing — and I hate that I'm thinking this — he hasn't actually DONE anything wrong. He's being polite. He's being helpful. He's being... exactly what an estate manager should be. And that's what bothers me. It's TOO right. Like the new kid who laughed too easy.

But no. No. I can't go there yet. I promised myself after that time with Terry — good bloke, Terry, turned out — that I'd give people a chance. Can't go around prickling at everyone. Sometimes a helpful bloke is just a helpful bloke.

Foxworth, though — 'personally invited by Lord Doily himself.' Was he now? That's a lot of puffing up for a man who just walked in. Claims to know where the treasure is. My gut doesn't prickle at him the same way. He's just... noise. Harmless noise.

Hartwell's gone for the guest book. Good lad. Thorough. Floor plans, county records, survey checklists — bit much, innit? But his heart's in the right place. He noticed the chandelier too. The way it lists northeast. I should keep an eye on that — Clara was standing right under it a moment ago.

Speaking of which — that chandelier. It's proper dodgy. If it came down while Clara was underneath... my stomach just clenched. I need to make sure she stays clear of it. Maybe I should have a closer look at it. Or better yet, get between her and it.

The guest book. Hartwell's already interacting with it. Might be worth having a look myself — see who's been here before. Could tell us something about this place. But I don't want to crowd the man.

My body's doing the thing where it's tracking two people at once — eyes flicking between Clara and Marsh, checking the distance between them. She's safe for now. Everyone's in the hall together. That's good. I can see everyone.

I think... I think I should check that chandelier. If it's dangerous, I need to know. And if something goes wrong, I need to be the one standing under it, not Clara.

events.desc: Listen to me, trying to be subtle. About as subtle as a brick through a window. But I had to ask. The way Pemberton said 'prepared' — it sat in my ear wrong. Like when someone says 'it's fine' and you know it ain't fine. I can't accuse the man of nothing. He's done nothing wrong. But my neck knows what my mouth can't say.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: I say, Vincent — or should I say Pemberton? Fascinating place you've kept here. You know, when Lord Doily showed me around, he was particularly proud of the kitchen. Kept going on about some hidden compartment behind the wood-burning stove. Something about the family silver being walled up during the war. I'd start there if I were any of you — but then again, I already know where the *real* prize is, so do carry on. I shall be in the library, consulting the inscription on the mantelpiece. Lord Doily mentioned it was the key to everything, and I'm sure I can crack it in minutes.
events.thinking:
The guest book interaction didn't reveal much — just the act of signing in. But the real data is in what I overheard. Vincent Marsh is calling himself Pemberton the estate manager — interesting, he's positioning himself as the insider, the authority figure. That's MY role. My jaw tightens slightly. events.thinking: Torn pages. James saw it too — pages ripped clean out of the guest book. My fingers find the ragged edges where the paper was pulled and something tightens behind my eyes, that pressure, the locked-box gravity. Who tears pages from a guest book? Someone who didn't want their visit recorded. Or someone who wanted to erase someone else's visit. The prickling spreads from my scalp down the back of my neck. This is the seam — the thing that doesn't fit. But everyone's moving. Vincent — Pemberton — whoever he is right now — has already gone to the library. Reginald's strutted off claiming he'll crack the inscription in minutes, bless him. James went too. And here I am with the Boys and a mutilated guest book, my fingers warm against the torn edges, the cave-mouth feeling pulling me toward the library where the inscription waits. But Danny's asking the right questions — 'prepared' like tidied, or 'prepared' like set up. My stomach does that small protective clench, the bridge-building instinct. The Boys are looking out for me the way they always do. The way they promised Daddy. I need to move — the library is where the puzzle is, and half the group is already there. But I'm filing those torn pages away. Someone went to trouble over this book, and that means it matters. My feet are already pointed toward the library door.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Here we are, gentlemen — the heart of the manor, as the late master would say. Now, the inscription on the mantelpiece has been there since the house was built, or so I'm told. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Visitors have puzzled over it for years. I confess, I'm merely the estate manager — riddles are rather above my station. But I have noticed something curious about the bookshelves... several volumes appear to have been shelved upside down. Carelessness, perhaps? Or perhaps the late master had his reasons. He was a most particular gentleman.
events.thinking:
The library. My breathing slows the moment I cross the threshold. The tall ceilings, the dust motes suspended in the thin light — this room feels like the inside of a mind. My mind.

The inscription on the mantelpiece. I can read it from here: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is a map. My fingers twitch — I knew before I finished reading. The riddle is child's play. But the question is: what does knowing it unlock? The mantelpiece itself must have a mechanism.

Reginald followed me in. Of course he did — greedy, impulsive, blustering about Lord Doily and brandy. He's already examining the inscription, no doubt. And James — methodical James, right behind. Both of them here. Clara is NOT here. She's still in the entrance hall with the Brixton Boys.

That changes things. Clara is separated from me — which is both problem and opportunity. Problem: I can't monitor her. Opportunity: I can work the library without her protectors watching me closely. But wait — James IS here. He's watching. He notices things. The torn pages in the guest book — he spotted that.

The Brixton Boys asked me directly what I meant by 'prepared.' That prickle at my neck again. Danny asks questions. Danny watches. I need to address that — but later, when I can calibrate the response.

For now: the riddle. The answer is a map. But I must not solve it too quickly — Pemberton is helpful but not brilliant. He wouldn't know. He'd defer to the guests. Let Reginald or James work it out, or guide them close enough that they feel clever. Meanwhile, I need to examine the mantelpiece itself. There may be a hidden compartment, a lever, something the riddle unlocks. If I can find it first and conceal it...

No. Too elaborate already. My constraint — I over-prepare. Keep it simple. Read the inscription openly. Let the others puzzle over it. Examine the bookshelves for anything useful — several books are upside down, which is a signal. Someone placed them that way deliberately. That's the real clue.

But the mantelpiece first. Interact with it. See what Pemberton would naturally do — present it to the guests, gesture toward it, accidentally brush against the stone. An estate manager would know this room intimately.

events.desc: A map. The answer is a map. I solved it before my second breath in this room. But Pemberton wouldn't know that — poor, dutiful Pemberton, who dusts the shelves and keeps the accounts and never once looks up from his station. Let them wrestle with the riddle while I examine what really matters — those upside-down books are practically screaming. The late master was particular, yes. Particularly fond of hiding things in plain sight. Rather like me.

I've studied Victorian engineering — these old manors are riddled with concealed compartments. And I notice several books on these shelves have been placed upside down. That's no accident. I intend to examine every last one of them. Pemberton, has anyone else attempted this riddle before us?

The upside-down books — those need cataloguing too. Someone arranged them that way. A code? Page numbers? Spine letters?

I'm over-preparing again. I can feel it happening. The elaborate plan forming: cross-reference the upside-down book titles, solve the riddle, check the stonework for hidden compartments, document everything, present findings to Clara in an organized dossier. That's... that's too much. But my hands are already reaching for the first upside-down book.

Pemberton is watching. My neck prickles. Give him the benefit of the doubt. Father would.
